newsitem.title: USA: Regional trade driving Asia-Pacific air growth.
newsitem.headline: Regional trade driving Asia-Pacific air growth.

text.p: The phenomenal growth of air transport experienced by Asia-Pacific airlines is increasingly driven by an upsurge in intra-regional trade, Orient Airlines Association(OAA) commercial director Carlos Chua said.

He told an IATA conference on Tuesday that increased economic activity coupled with greater mobility of labour amongst the Asia-Pacific economies would sustain air travel growth at current levels for at least another five years.

Over the seven-year period (1989-95) capacity among OAA members -- which groups 16 leading Asian airlines -- had risen 70 percent from 354 billion available seat kilometres to 613 billion in 1995/96 and had been accompanied by a 62 percent rise in revenue passenger kilometres.

While this had seen an easing in load factors from 73 percent in 1990 to a present-day 68 percent, the industry had enjoyed average yields of 79 cents per revenue tonne kilometre over the past two years.
"This profit came mainly from the cost side rather than the revenue side," said Chua.

"It was also been greatly helped by an appreciation in the yen experienced by our two Japanese member carriers (Japan Airlines Co Ltd and All Nippon Airways ) who, because of their size, tend to sway the yield."
Despite good average returns, he added, "our group is dominated by a few profitable carriers at a time when quite a few smaller members also lost money."
Chua said there was a clear corollary in his view between regional gross domestic product(GDP), trade and revenue passenger kilometres which augured well for air transport within Asia-Pacific.

While average GDP growth predictions for the world were 3.2 percent for 1996 and 3.5 percent for 1997, most OAA economies were on the high side of single digit performance ranging from 8 percent for Thailand and 7.5 percent for Singapore down to 4.5 percent for Hong Kong and one percent for Papua New Guinea.
But Chua questioned whether the region's airports were ready for this level of growth, highlighting relatively poor on-time performance at many key airports.
"New airports are under construction in Hong Kong, Bangkok, Seoul, Kuala Lumpur and Manila to cope with this growth," said the OAA official.
"But airport planners need to be brought into the wider planning process along with the airlines and the aircraft manufacturers to avoid downstream problems," he added.
